brief.text: What we en­gage with, book or phone, changes the brain it­self, Amit Varma said. London’s taxi driv­ers had their brains rewired once they re­lied on maps. {#taxi}

brief.head: Ten-letter words
brief.text: Children who hear ten-letter words from birth to five, Varma said, cit­ing Jim Heckman, gain a layer of in­tel­li­gence that can­not be made up later. {120-R06}

brief.text: In the con­cen­tra­tion camps, Viktor Frankl wrote, lit­er­a­ture gave in­mates so­lace. It tells us, Varma said, that we are not alone, and that this too shall pass. {120-C04}

brief.head: Go down rabbit holes
brief.text: When a sub­ject grabs you, Varma said, chase the foot­notes, ask ChatGPT, check Wikipedia and buy the next book. “Do not think of these as di­gres­sions.” {120-C13}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on why, and how, to read
lead.head: Booked for life

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 120

body: Amit Varma opened with a les­son in close read­ing. To be a huge fan of hood­ies, he ex­plained, is to be huge, and a fan of hood­ies. “A care­ful read­ing will re­ward you with ad­di­tional mean­ing and lay­ers.” {120-J01}

The rest of the episode was a primer in three parts: why to read, how to build the habit, and how to read a book. Ajay Shah played the busy scep­tic, too oc­cu­pied scrolling Instagram to read. Varma promised that within min­utes Shah would delete the app and be­come a ded­i­cated reader.
## The case for books
Varma of­fered eleven rea­sons to read. The num­ber was no risk, he said, “be­cause Ajay can’t count, but Amit can.”

The first was that read­ing sup­plies the dots we con­nect to pic­ture the world. Experience shows only the present, and a nar­row slice of it. “The more dots we have, the more high def­i­ni­tion our pic­ture,” he said. {120-C01}
Shah put it an­other way. A prac­ti­cal per­son reaches sev­enty with the knowl­edge of one life. A reader taps the knowl­edge of hun­dreds or thou­sands.

Reading, Varma went on, is good for the brain, the heart and the psy­che. It makes bet­ter cit­i­zens and more cre­ative writ­ers, car­ries a con­ver­sa­tion across time and builds a lat­tice­work of men­tal mod­els. It saves soli­tude from lone­li­ness, gives joy, and helps you know your­self.
Shah added a cau­tion: read­ing does not guar­an­tee good­ness. Joseph Stalin, he said, was very well read.
## The habit
Wanting to read is the easy part. “I think the key word here which I want to em­pha­sise is habit,” Varma said.

Start small, he ad­vised, read often rather than long, tie read­ing to an ex­ist­ing rou­tine, keep books within reach and find fel­low read­ers. Above all, begin with iden­tity: if the best ver­sion of you is a reader, be that per­son. {120-C10}
## Reading the book

For non­fic­tion, Varma turned to Mortimer Adler’s four lev­els of read­ing, which run from mak­ing sense of sen­tences to read­ing many books on a sin­gle sub­ject. {120-R01} For fic­tion, he fol­lowed Harold Bloom: slow down, and never skim.
He ended with four clos­ing thoughts. Format doesn’t mat­ter. It is fine to quit a book. Reading is not a com­pe­ti­tion. And iden­tity comes first.
On quit­ting, he of­fered a sum. An op­ti­mistic life ex­pectancy, times an op­ti­mistic num­ber of books a year, gives the most you will ever read: a piti­ful frac­tion of all that ex­ists.
Shah, by his own ac­count “the world’s slow­est reader”, reads pages slowly but deeply. Reading well, he ar­gued, is like eat­ing well: eas­ier as a house­hold than alone.

Both hosts bris­tled at AI sum­maries of books. “Books are not in­for­ma­tion,” Shah said. {120-C19} What mat­ters, he said, is the ten or twenty hours of in­ti­mate con­ver­sa­tion with one great au­thor.
Varma closed by show­ing how he takes notes on a book, chap­ter by chap­ter and theme by theme, in an app called Roam Research.

second.label: Reading and goodness
second.head: Marginalia of a monster
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why reading is no guarantee of goodness

pic.caption: Official portrait of Joseph Stalin issued for his 70th birthday in 1949

body: By read­ing, Ajay Shah said, we im­pose a pos­i­tive ex­ter­nal­ity on the world, mak­ing those around us think and de­bate bet­ter. {120-C06} But read­ing is not a suf­fi­cient con­di­tion for good­ness.

His ex­hibit was Joseph Stalin, whom he ranked history’s sec­ond-worst mon­ster, after Chairman Mao and ahead of Hitler. {120-S03} Citing, he thought, Stephen Kotkin, Shah said Stalin could have held an hour’s com­fort­able con­ver­sa­tion with any philoso­pher. He read in­ten­sively and scrib­bled in his books.

Amit Varma added Mao, a foun­da­tional thinker on guer­rilla war­fare; Shah stressed that Mao had the­o­rised his way there. That, Varma said, was like Shah the­o­ris­ing about the world and then doing a YouTube show. “Those who can do,” Shah replied, “the oth­ers be­come pod­cast­ers.” {120-J03}

quote.text: He was con­sid­ered an ex­tremely so­phis­ti­cated and eru­dite per­son. He was very well read.

third.head: Summary judgment

pic.caption: Amit Varma on AI summaries of books

body: On a drive in DC last year, a friend proudly told Amit Varma that he had AI make 500-word sum­maries of Varma’s eight-hour episodes of *The Seen and the Unseen*. {120-S11} He ex­pected ap­proval, and did the same with books.

“I was lit­er­ally vis­cer­ally angry, not be­cause it’s my show,” Varma said, “but be­cause that’s such a stupid way of con­sum­ing knowl­edge.” A book, he said, teaches you how to think, and there is no short­cut for that.

Ajay Shah, cit­ing a New York Times pod­cast con­ver­sa­tion by Ezra Klein, had noted that a thou­sand-word sum­mary can make you look so­phis­ti­cated at a cock­tail party. {#cocktail} We read, he said, for the hours of in­ti­mate con­ver­sa­tion with the au­thor.
“Books are not in­for­ma­tion,” Shah said. “Information is triv­ial. You can look it up.” {120-C19}

box.title: The guide behind part three
box.text: *How to Read a Book* by Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren sets out four lev­els of read­ing, and a four-step method for chew­ing a book: clas­sify it, state its gist, out­line its parts, name its prob­lem. {120-R01}

sections.label: Part One
sections.head: Eleven reasons to open a book
sections.caption: eleven reasons to read
body: Amit Varma gave eleven rea­sons to read, and the first was about dots. We paint pic­tures of the world by con­nect­ing them, he said, and the more we have, the sharper the pic­ture. {120-C01}

Experience alone can­not sup­ply them. A friend who knew Narendra Modi told Varma how Modi once wept re­call­ing a child­hood night when his mother was ill and hot, and he flicked the fan switch to find no elec­tric­ity. Modi grasped power and roads be­cause he had lived them, Varma said. But spon­ta­neous order can­not be seen with your own eyes. {120-S02}
Ajay Shah put it in lives: a prac­ti­cal doer reaches sev­enty with one life’s knowl­edge, a reader with that of thou­sands.
## Brain, heart and psy­che

Reading is good for the brain, Varma said: scrolling hops from fac­toid to fac­toid, while books build con­nec­tions. It is good for the heart, be­cause read­ing ex­pands what Martha Nussbaum calls nar­ra­tive imag­i­na­tion. {120-C03}
Shah re­called read­ing that Tolstoy, writ­ing *War and Peace*, walked around his house sob­bing un­con­trol­lably, lost in the minds of his char­ac­ters. {120-S04}

Reading also makes for in­formed cit­i­zens, feeds cre­ativ­ity and car­ries a con­ver­sa­tion across time. It builds what Charlie Munger called a lat­tice­work of mod­els, which, Varma said, is where the show gets its name. {120-C09}
~ And it saves soli­tude from lone­li­ness, brings joy and helps you know your­self.

quote.text: George Eliot called read­ing the near­est thing to life.

sections.label: Part Two
sections.head: Identity first, pages second
sections.caption: building a reading habit
body: The key word, Amit Varma said, is habit. Don’t set your­self a tar­get, such as fin­ish­ing a prize-winner. James Clear, in *Atomic Habits*, calls habits the com­pound in­ter­est of self-improvement.
Be bloody-minded for at least three months, Varma ad­vised, until the loop is hard­wired in the basal gan­glia and read­ing feels au­to­matic. {#threemonths}

Better still, start from iden­tity. Ask who the best ver­sion of you is. If that per­son reaches for a book in­stead of a phone, ac­tions flow from the self-image, and a missed day does not break you. {120-C10}
## Small, often, an­chored
Start small, with two pages or fif­teen min­utes. “Frequency mat­ters more than du­ra­tion,” Varma said, and Ajay Shah laughed. {120-J08}

Anchor read­ing to a rou­tine such as morn­ing cof­fee or the com­mute, be­cause neu­rons that fire to­gether wire to­gether. Keep books ev­ery­where, put the Kindle app up front and take the so­cial media apps out. {#kindle}

~ Decide in ad­vance what to read next, to spare your­self de­ci­sion fa­tigue. Reward your­self, as James Clear’s writer did by mov­ing a hair­pin be­tween jars for every para­graph. {120-R10} And find a com­mu­nity of read­ers.

quote.text: But my slo­gan for you would be just be it.

sections.label: Part Three
sections.head: Tasted, swallowed, chewed
sections.caption: how to read a book
body: Amit Varma drew his guide to the act of read­ing from three books, be­gin­ning with Mortimer Adler’s *How to Read a Book* and its four lev­els of read­ing. {120-R01}

Elementary read­ing is mak­ing sense of sen­tences. Inspectional read­ing is a first date with the book: the con­tents, the pref­ace, a skim to see whether it is re­ally an essay padded out, as many non­fic­tion books are. Francis Fukuyama’s *The End of History and the Last Man*, Varma said, is a rare book that goes well be­yond its essay. {120-R13}

Analytical read­ing means chew­ing: clas­sify the book, state its gist, out­line its parts and name the prob­lem the au­thor is try­ing to solve. Synoptical read­ing means many books on one sub­ject; Varma read some thirty for two episodes on Gandhi. {120-S08}
## Slow down for sto­ries

Fiction, Varma said, fol­low­ing Harold Bloom’s *How to Read and Why*, should never be skimmed. Short sto­ries favour the tacit and make the reader dis­cern what the writer leaves out. Memorise poems. {120-C14} Read a Shakespeare play, watch it, then read it again.
~ Francine Prose’s *Reading Like a Writer* adds an eye for the author’s tools, from the clipped sen­tences of hard-boiled crime fic­tion to Saramago’s pages-long ones.

quote.text: Some books are to be tasted, oth­ers to be swal­lowed, and some few to be chewed and di­gested.
quote.who: Francis Bacon, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Closing thoughts
sections.head: Drop the book, not the habit
sections.caption: quitting books, and other closing thoughts
body: Format doesn’t mat­ter, Amit Varma said. “Literature is words. That’s what they are. Everything else is pack­ag­ing.” Insisting on phys­i­cal books shows nos­tal­gia, not love of lit­er­a­ture. {120-C15}
Audiobooks are a some­what dif­fer­ent ex­pe­ri­ence, since you can­not eas­ily stop and reread. But they let some­one hang­ing on a local train spend that half-hour with words.
## A life­time bud­get

It is fine to quit a book. Multiply an op­ti­mistic life ex­pectancy by an op­ti­mistic num­ber of books a year, and the an­swer is piti­fully small be­side the mil­lions writ­ten. “Don’t throw good time after bad,” he said. {120-C16}
Don’t feel guilty about aban­don­ing a prize-winner ev­ery­one loves, and don’t be a snob: an air­port best­seller or an aca­demic paper is fine if it brings en­joy­ment or en­light­en­ment.

Nor is read­ing a com­pe­ti­tion. Varma once said, quite hon­estly, that he had read two hun­dred books in a year, and was abused on Twitter for show­ing off. He has not men­tioned a num­ber since. {120-S09}
~ His speed, he said, comes from a habit begun at three or four. What mat­ters is the time spent in a con­tem­pla­tive state, not the score.

quote.text: There is no Olympics of read­ing.

sections.label: Ajay’s additions
sections.head: Slow and deep, and together
sections.caption: reading slowly, and reading together
body: Ajay Shah had a con­fes­sion. He reads with only one mode, slowly, play­ing with every sen­tence, word and ar­gu­ment. He would like to read three times the pa­pers and ten times the books he does. {120-S10}
He has stopped fight­ing it. Everything that has hap­pened to him, he said, has come out of read­ing this way, though he is not say­ing it is good for ev­ery­one.
## A house­hold of read­ers

His sec­ond point was about food. In a house­hold where junk food is bought and white rice comes out of the kitchen, eat­ing healthy takes a su­per­hu­man ef­fort, so mod­ern think­ing on nu­tri­tion changes the whole food en­vi­ron­ment. Reading well, like eat­ing well, is harder alone. {120-C18}
Viewers have told him the best way to watch the show is in a group that hits pause at every chap­ter break to argue. {#groupview} That turns pas­sive con­sump­tion into ac­tive learn­ing.
Amit Varma won­dered what such groups might be say­ing. Perhaps: “How would the show look with two Ajays talk­ing to each other?” {120-J14}
~ When three peo­ple in the room dis­agree and talk it out, Shah said, the knowl­edge be­comes their own.

quote.text: I’m the world’s slow­est reader. I read pages slowly, but I read them deeply.

art.caption: Amit Varma on reading slowly, and reading together

sections.label: Amit’s method
sections.head: Mapping the territory
sections.caption: taking notes in Roam Research
body: Amit Varma closed with a demon­stra­tion of how he takes notes on a book in Roam Research, an app he loves for its nested en­tries and bidi­rec­tional links.

Reading Ghazala Wahab’s *Born a Muslim* for an episode, he first set down the chap­ter ti­tles as top-level en­tries, then nested every point be­neath them and every quote a level deeper. One was a beau­ti­ful ex­am­ple of show, don’t tell: a grand­fa­ther who, in win­ter, shelled pine nuts dur­ing the day to re­ward the chil­dren in the evening. {#pinenuts}
Earlier, he said, he kept sixty pages of Microsoft Word and scrolled fran­ti­cally. {120-C20} Now any term in dou­ble brack­ets be­comes a link that gath­ers every re­lated quote.
## A layer of themes

When ma­te­rial has no chap­ters, he builds a struc­ture of his own. Mahima Vashisht, one of his writ­ing stu­dents, had writ­ten more than a hun­dred posts of her news­let­ter, *Womaning in India*. {#hundredposts}

Varma listed the posts, then opened a sec­tion called themes: con­trol­ling fe­male sex­u­al­ity, stereo­types, a world de­signed by men, for men. That let him ap­proach her ma­te­rial the­mat­i­cally.
~ The method works even with­out a pod­cast to pre­pare, he said. “Now I un­der­stand the ter­ri­tory.”

quote.text: No, bro. I’m kind of read­ing them out from this.

We read books be­cause for that du­ra­tion of ten hours or twenty hours, we are with the au­thor in an in­ti­mate con­ver­sa­tion. We are grap­pling with the ar­gu­ment, we are grap­pling with com­plex ideas.

p3.title: Tales from the shelf
p3.deck: A snooze skipped, a father’s gift, a jar of paperclips and a poker face

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the book he found by accident
stories.head: Searched for Bloom, found Virtue
body: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah shoot about six episodes in three days, and this was the sixth. The night be­fore, Varma went to bed super tired and super stressed about the prep still to be done.

Before sleep­ing, he switched on his iPad and searched his Kindle for “Bloom”, mean­ing only to keep Harold Bloom’s book ready, not even to read it. The search also turned up books pub­lished by Bloomsbury. {#bloomsbury}

One was Alasdair MacIntyre’s *After Virtue*. Suyash Rai, a dear friend of the hosts and, Varma said, a great thinker, had rec­om­mended it a long time ago; MacIntyre is a great in­flu­ence on him. Varma bought the book im­me­di­ately, and then did not read it.

A few weeks ear­lier, Pratap Bhanu Mehta had taken him to lunch in Bombay and spo­ken of MacIntyre, who had died in May. That was an­other prick in his head: “dude, what are you doing? You gotta read this guy.”
That night he read the first chap­ter and half of the sec­ond be­fore sleep won. He woke with the ar­gu­ment run­ning through his head.
“I typ­i­cally will hit Snooze 17 times be­fore I get up,” he said. “But I kinda jumped out of bed be­cause I was like, I have to read the book.” {120-S05}
~ Later, over cof­fee at the din­ing table, he read on in­stead of prep­ping for this episode. He had to know how the chap­ter fin­ished.
stories.why: Serendipity and plea­sure, not duty, drive a read­ing life. Ideas books, Varma said, can ex­pand the brain and grip you as hard as sto­ries do. When one has that ef­fect on you, em­brace it.
stories.postscript: Varma had gone look­ing for Harold Bloom’s *How to Read and Why*, which he went on to rec­om­mend in the episode. {120-R02}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the book that beat his snooze button

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on his father’s sixty volumes
stories.head: Great Books, kept for a father
body: Amit Varma’s fa­ther owned the sixty-volume *Great Books of the Western World*. For about ten years be­fore he died, he kept telling his son to take it to Bombay: “This is for you. I re­ally want you to have this.”
Varma kept re­fus­ing. “In Bombay, the cost of a book is not what you pay for it, but the real es­tate it oc­cu­pies,” he said. His lit­tle rented house had no space. {120-S07}
After his fa­ther died, his li­brary of many thou­sands of books went to a com­mu­nity li­brary. Varma kept the sixty, as a mem­ory of his dad.

~ The two he does read sit on his desk: the Synopticon, Mortimer Adler’s es­says on themes like love, death and de­sire across the whole canon. “It fills me with such awe, it fills me with such joy.” {#awe}
stories.why: Books can be kept out of love rather than use. The Synopticon also shows syn­op­ti­cal read­ing at work: one quote, Varma said, can send him straight to an­other author’s vol­ume, as when he found a line from Nietzsche.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his father’s Great Books

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a colleague’s cure for constant interruptions
stories.head: The price of a question
body: At NIPFP, Ila Patnaik was ir­ri­tated that the admin team kept com­ing to her for de­ci­sions it could make it­self. Her view, as Ajay Shah put it: “I have no great value added in what needs to be done, you fig­ure it out.”
Her so­lu­tion was a jar. “Each time you come to me to ask me a ques­tion, you have to put one paper clip into this jar,” Shah said. “It worked dra­mat­i­cally.” {120-S06}
People would put in a pa­per­clip, hang their heads in shame, and then ask. The flow of rub­bish in­ter­rup­tions fell dra­mat­i­cally, and the team be­came more thought­ful.
~ Amit Varma re­called the fa­mous thought ex­per­i­ment in AI about a pa­per­clip max­imiser. “It turns out that Ila is a pa­per­clip min­imiser,” he said. {120-J11}
stories.why: A tiny, vis­i­ble cost can change be­hav­iour more than a lec­ture. It makes peo­ple pause and ask whether a ques­tion is re­ally worth ask­ing: gam­i­fi­ca­tion, run in re­verse. Ajay Shah told it as a trick for build­ing habits.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Ila Patnaik’s paperclip jar

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on tells, smiles and hiding his face
stories.head: Poker face, under a hood
body: Amit Varma be­came a fan of hood­ies when he was a pro­fes­sional poker player, be­tween 2010 and 2015. {#poker} Poker is fun­da­men­tally maths, he said, but in live games you can give away tells.

So after bet­ting he would cover his face, avoid eye con­tact, look at the table and keep ev­ery­thing ex­actly the same, bluff­ing or not. Opponents watch for di­lat­ing pupils or a puls­ing carotid artery.

His own favourite tell was a joke. “Human be­ings have two kinds of smiles,” he said. “There’s a fake smile and a gen­uine smile.” A gen­uine smile means a player is com­fort­able; a fake one means he is wor­ried. {120-S01}
~ Even then, Varma said, you only up­date your pri­ors a lit­tle. The man with the fake smile might just have a great hand, and an ur­gent need for the loo.
stories.why: Since sig­nals leak, the dis­ci­plined player shuts the chan­nel en­tirely, show­ing the same blank pos­ture every time. And no tell, how­ever re­li­able, set­tles any­thing: it only nudges a judge­ment that re­mains un­cer­tain.
stories.postscript: He opened by pars­ing his own sen­tence: being “a huge fan of hood­ies” means he is huge, and a fan of hood­ies. {120-J01}

quiz.q: Which four levels of reading does Mortimer Adler describe in *How to Read a Book*?
quiz.a: Elementary, in­spec­tional, an­a­lyt­i­cal and syn­op­ti­cal: from sen­tences to many books on one sub­ject.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma refuse, for about ten years, to take his father’s sixty volumes to Bombay?
quiz.a: In Bombay, a book’s real cost is the real es­tate it oc­cu­pies.

quiz.q: What did Ila Patnaik make her admin team do before asking her a question?
quiz.a: Drop a pa­per­clip into a jar, which cut triv­ial in­ter­rup­tions dra­mat­i­cally.

quiz.q: What does Harold Bloom, as Amit Varma reported, advise readers to do with poems?
quiz.a: Memorise them, so the poem pos­sesses you and you can read it more closely.

quiz.q: How does Amit Varma work out your lifetime book budget, and what follows from it?
quiz.a: Multiply op­ti­mistic life ex­pectancy by books a year; the total is small, so quit freely.

quiz.q: According to Amit Varma, where does the show’s name, *Everything is Everything*, come from?
quiz.a: Reading re­veals the in­ter­con­nect­ed­ness of ev­ery­thing, even fields of study kept in sep­a­rate silos.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 120. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Leo Tolstoy (Sergei Prokudin-Gorskii, public domain); Mortimer J. Adler (Center for the Study of The Great Ideas, CC BY-SA 3.0); Joseph Stalin (Ivan Shagin, public domain); Harold Bloom (Gotfryd, Bernard, photographer, public domain); Virginia Woolf (George Charles Beresford / Adam Cuerden, public domain); Viktor Frankl (Prof. Dr. Franz Vesely, CC BY-SA 3.0 de). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: How to Read a Book
shelf.creator: Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren
shelf.why: Lays out the four lev­els of read­ing (el­e­men­tary, in­spec­tional, an­a­lyt­i­cal, syn­op­ti­cal).

shelf.title: How to Read and Why
shelf.creator: Harold Bloom
shelf.why: Bloom ex­plains what at­ti­tude each genre de­mands.

shelf.title: Reading Like a Writer
shelf.creator: Francine Prose
shelf.why: Teaches you to no­tice the author’s tools, such as why one word and not an­other, and how sen­tence length builds rhythm or im­mer­sion.

shelf.title: Is Google Making Us Stupid?
shelf.creator: Nicholas Carr
shelf.why: Argues that our shal­low in­ter­ac­tion with the in­ter­net keeps us from going deep and makes us stu­pider, while books pull the other way.

shelf.title: The Shallows
shelf.creator: Nicholas Carr
shelf.why: A rare essay-turned-book that earns its length.

shelf.title: Jim Heckman’s work (The Heckman Equation)
shelf.creator: Jim Heckman
shelf.why: Hard-nosed re­turn-on-investment ev­i­dence that the big­gest pay­offs come from in­ter­ven­tions at ages 0 to 5, es­pe­cially for dis­ad­van­taged chil­dren: hear­ing com­plex ‘ten-letter words’ early builds a layer of in­tel­li­gence that can’t be made up later.

shelf.title: Man’s Search for Meaning
shelf.creator: Viktor Frankl
shelf.why: Frankl records that for con­cen­tra­tion-camp in­mates, lit­er­a­ture, whether held, re­mem­bered or dis­cussed, gave so­lace and a sense that the present mo­ment is not all there is.

shelf.title: After Virtue
shelf.creator: Alasdair MacIntyre
shelf.why: Amit loved it so much he woke with its ar­gu­ment in his head and read it over break­fast in­stead of prep­ping.

shelf.title: Suyash Rai Embraces India’s Complexity (Ep 307, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Suyash Rai
shelf.why: A way into the mind of Suyash Rai, whom Amit re­gards as a great thinker, deeply in­flu­enced by Alasdair MacIntyre, on dharma, India’s com­plex­ity and the lim­its of the state.

shelf.title: Atomic Habits
shelf.creator: James Clear
shelf.why: The best book on pro­duc­tiv­ity Amit has read, and the one to start with if you read only one: turn your mind from goals to habits and pro­cesses, the com­pound in­ter­est of self-improvement, and use small re­wards to make habits stick.

shelf.title: chickenhappyhour on Instagram (and Amit’s favourite chicken video)
shelf.why: Amit finds them ‘mind blowing’ and watches his favourite on loop.

shelf.title: The Paris Review Book for Planes, Trains, Elevators, and Waiting Rooms
shelf.creator: The Paris Review
shelf.why: Its sto­ries run from el­e­va­tor-ride length to long-haul-flight length.

shelf.title: The End of History and the Last Man (and the essay ‘The End of History?’)
shelf.creator: Francis Fukuyama
shelf.why: A rare case where the book is gen­uinely great and goes well be­yond the essay it grew from.

shelf.title: Understanding Gandhi, Parts 1 and 2 (Eps 104–105, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ramachandra Guha
shelf.why: Amit’s first two episodes with Ramachandra Guha, on Gandhi, for which Amit read some thirty books, so they dis­til a whole shelf of bi­ogra­phies.

shelf.title: The Good Boatman
shelf.creator: Rajmohan Gandhi
shelf.why: Thematic es­says on Gandhi’s life, from women to caste, that syn­the­sise a vast amount of ma­te­rial: ‘a pow­er­ful book of ideas’ for en­gag­ing with his con­tra­dic­tions, and Amit’s model of a syn­op­tic book.

shelf.title: Great Books of the Western World (especially the Synopticon volumes)
shelf.creator: Mortimer Adler (editor)
shelf.why: Mortimer Adler’s set, whose the­matic es­says on death, love, de­sire, pur­pose and agency draw on the en­tire canon, fill Amit with awe and send him to the orig­i­nal au­thors.

shelf.title: How Should One Read a Book?
shelf.creator: Virginia Woolf
shelf.why: Amit calls it a great essay on ex­actly this episode’s ques­tion.

shelf.title: Aspects of the Novel
shelf.creator: E. M. Forster
shelf.why: It gives a great in­sight into a great novelist’s mind.

shelf.title: Why Read the Classics?
shelf.creator: Italo Calvino
shelf.why: Amit calls it an ex­cel­lent book on the case for the clas­sics.

shelf.title: How Fiction Works
shelf.creator: James Wood
shelf.why: Useful for read­ers, not just writ­ers.

shelf.title: The Pleasures of Reading in an Age of Distraction
shelf.creator: Alan Jacobs
shelf.why: A con­tem­po­rary take on read­ing well amid the dis­trac­tions this episode keeps fight­ing.

shelf.title: Lessons from an Ankhon Dekhi Prime Minister
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s case for read­ing: ex­pe­ri­ence gives us only a few dots, slowly, while books let us col­lect many dots fast, live many lives and reach deep, com­plex truths about the world that ex­pe­ri­ence alone can’t.

shelf.title: Ezra Klein interviewed by David Perell
shelf.creator: Ezra Klein and David Perell
shelf.why: Ajay says it ‘goes to the core’ of why we read.

shelf.title: Susan Thomas’s book club in Bombay
shelf.creator: Susan Thomas
shelf.why: An in-person read­ing com­mu­nity in Bombay.

shelf.title: Roam Research
shelf.why: Amit’s note-taking tool, which he calls a game changer: nested en­tries and two-way links turn any term into a hub of re­lated notes, re­plac­ing his scroll-and-search Word files and mak­ing up for a mem­ory he says isn’t great.

shelf.title: Being Muslim in India (Ep 216, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ghazala Wahab
shelf.why: Amit’s con­ver­sa­tion with Ghazala Wahab, which he holds up as a show­case of what his chap­ter-by-chapter note-taking pro­duces; her book also sup­plies a beau­ti­ful ex­am­ple of ‘show, don’t tell’.

shelf.title: Womaning in India With Mahima Vashisht (Ep 293, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Mahima Vashisht
shelf.why: Shows how build­ing your own themes layer turns a pile of ma­te­rial into a map of the ter­ri­tory, and how that made a the­matic con­ver­sa­tion pos­si­ble.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

laughs.text: Amit says ‘Frequency mat­ters more than duration’, and Ajay laughs. Amit: ‘You thought of sex again.’ Ajay: ‘Bro. Frequency mat­ters more than du­ra­tion. What else can I think of?’

On James Clear’s body­builder who moved a mar­ble be­tween jars for every set: ‘one sin­cerely hopes he never dropped his weights on his head be­cause then he might have lost his mar­bles... I keep mak­ing this joke. People keep laugh­ing, I don’t know why.’
Amit on com­mu­ni­ca­tion be­tween species: ‘Dogs will bark to each other, cats will meow to each other, es­pe­cially while con­fess­ing, you’ll have me­ow­pas.’
Montaigne: ‘I have no more made my book than my book has made me’, used for read­ing as self-discovery.

Hemingway’s ice­berg the­ory and ‘show, don’t tell’, il­lus­trated by Amit’s image of him­self at a win­dow as the light fades and his tea goes cold, un­drunk. Ghazala Wahab’s grand­fa­ther of­fers an­other: he shelled pine nuts all day to re­ward the grand­kids with fist­fuls in the evening, rather than her writ­ing ‘he loved us’.
